newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. urges India to press ahead with reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges India to press ahead with reforms.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday exhorted India to press ahead with more bold free-market reforms and launch a second "Green Revolution" to lift the fortunes of millions of impoverished farmers.
U.S. ambassador to India Frank Wisner urged India to commit at a meeting next month in Geneva to phasing out the import protection which it has enjoyed for more than four decades.

Wisner, who is set to leave the U.S. diplomatic corps in July, told the Confederation of Indian Industry at a farewell luncheon that India's trading partners wanted it to protect intellectual property rights such as patents and copyrights.
"That India's economic reform programme has accomplished much cannot be disputed," he said.
"Nor can the fact that much remains to be done. India will realise its potential only with boldness of vision and a determination to put policies into practice."

The envoy, who during his three-year tenure has spearheaded the U.S. drive to expand its business presence in India, urged New Delhi to set aside the trade protection it has enjoyed for more than 40 years under article 18 of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
The article has permitted India to impose "temporary" restrictions on a long list of imports.

Diplomats said the International Monetary Fund had concluded that the conditions which had justified the curbs -- shortage of exchange reserves and slow growth -- no longer existed, and trading partners were pressing India to phase out the controls.
Ahead of a meeting in Geneva set for early June, India announced a plan which would commit it to dismantling the trade restrictions progressively over nine years.
"It's a big disappointment," a Western diplomat said. "We had expected them to phase them out by 2000. It remains to be negotiated."
Venturing onto controversial terrain, Wisner reiterated a call for India to adopt a legal framework for protecting intellectual property.

Earlier this month, Washington kept India on a "watch list" of countries potentially subject to trade sanctions for alleged failure to protect intellectual property rights. Delhi denounced the decision to keep it on its "Special 301" list.

Wisner has recently drawn biting criticism in the Indian press for cautioning that the levels of foreign investment in India will depend to some degree on the extent to which foreign firms believe their intellectual property rights are shielded.
The U.S. ambassador praised India for its market-opening budget for 1997/98 (April-March) and for signing the Information Technology Agreement in the World Trade Organisation.
But he said more steps were needed to develop infrastructure, reduce the fiscal deficit, open up the financial sector, reduce trade barriers and invest in education.

Evoking the agricultural policies adopted in the 1960s which eventually made India self-sufficient in food, Wisner called for a second "Green Revolution" to bring irrigation to dry lands, spread bio-technology and alleviate rural poverty.
